rv.q: The final scene, where Beatrice and Benedick finally come together, is absolutely joyful.
This light-hearted take on Shakespeare’s story of matched wits and combative gender dynamics tells the familiar tale with maximum levity.
In Pippa Nixon’s Beatrice and Ken Nwosu’s Benedick, it gives us one of the most charming accounts of Shakespeare’s sparring partners this decade.
It’s the more serious bits where it struggles.
But it is not quite as keen to lean in to the problematic elements of the play.
Ultimately what we’re left with is the taste of love games that can all too easily become bittersweet.

All is put right in time for the sort of collectively joyful curtain call that defines the Globe at its very best, of which this Much Ado – opening just in time for the summer solstice – is a shining example.
Chelsea Walker’s Much Ado is a triumphant joy.
Chelsea Walker pulls Hero out of the tragic shadows by switching a few lines and adding a scene in which Hero confronts the returned Don John.
And it is a delight on a summer’s evening: a delicately calibrated and confident treat.
All the comic effects are skilfully handled.
This version is hugely enjoyable, even if some of the darker intent doesn’t quite pack the punch that it could.

The Globe's production may not have the star pulling power of Jamie Lloyd's 2025 production at Drury Lane (which boasted Tom Hiddleston and the magnificent Hayley Atwell) but it's still a joyfully boisterous crowd pleaser despite a few issues in vocal projection.
Yet the glorious swoop of their acidic romance is offset by a portrayal of the “love” story between Hero and Claudio as something much more disturbing.

This version of Shakespeare’s classic deception comedy manages to be both minimalist and maximalist at once, starting with an ensemble of costumes ranging from TikTok-favoured butter yellow sundresses to BDSM harnesses, by way of sharp 1970s tailoring, offering a confused sense of time and place.
This is a sublime production of Much Ado About Nothing that captures the hearts and minds of its audience.
All in all, this is a triumphant production from Shakespeare’s Globe: heartfelt, hilarious, and immensely entertaining.
Walker’s command of the tonal shift is assured: we are laughing one minute and stunned into silence by the brutality of the accusations the next.
Walker’s direction is a masterclass in smooth storytelling.
A fun and feisty adaptation of a summer classic.
She is on solid but less than inspired form here.
The skilled direction and talented cast inject fun and vibrancy into this entertaining production.

Chelsea Walker’s Much Ado About Nothing succeeds because it trusts Shakespeare’s text while illuminating its enduring relevance, producing a comedy that feels both timeless and thoroughly contemporary.

cn.t: Walker's contemporary Globe production delights with Nixon and Nwosu's sparkling chemistry as Beatrice and Benedick, though critics note tonal inconsistencies. Most praise its accessible, summery energy while some find it lacks depth.
